newsitem.title: FRANCE: Young Catholics stream into Paris to await Pope.
newsitem.headline: Young Catholics stream into Paris to await Pope.

text.p: Weighed down with backpacks and sleeping bags, tens of thousands of young Roman Catholics from around the world streamed into Paris on Monday ahead of Pope John Paul's visit later this week.
Singing, clapping, strumming guitars, or exhausted after long trips on special buses and trains, they were met by young volunteers in green t-shirts and straw hats.

More than 300,000 young people are expected in the French capital for the week-long 12th World Youth Days, a religious festival which includes several encounters with the pontiff, due in on Thursday for a four-day visit.
Half a million people are foreseen attending the festival's closing ceremony, a vast open-air mass to be celebrated by John Paul II at the Longchamp racetrack on the western outskirts of Paris.

Organisers have revised down the expected numbers, disappointed by the turnout of just 70,000 youths from France -- a reflection of a crisis of religious confidence in the country dubbed "the Church's eldest daughter" for its early mediaeval conversion to Catholicism.
But the chief organiser, Bishop Michel Dubost, was upbeat on Monday, saying many French pilgrims had registered late.
He told reporters 160 countries would be represented, and the number of pilgrims would easily reach 350,000.
The last World Youth Days, held in Manila two years ago, drew four million people.
With the French capital in the grip of a pollution alert thanks to a heatwave, the pilgrims' buses stopped on the outskirts to avoid exacerbating soaring ozone levels, caused mainly by exhaust fumes.

Authorities have asked motorists to use public transport, and lowered speed limits on the Peripherique orbital motorway. They have advised children, the elderly and people with respiratory ailments to stay at home.
Dubost said organisers had taken all steps necessary to ensure the pope, a frail 77, could cope with the heat and exhaustion of a packed schedule.
"I am not sure he will heed all our advice. I believe he works more than normal at his age, and he listens less than he should to advice of caution," he told reporters.

As they were despatched to host families, school dormitories and camp sites, pilgrims were handed blue bags containing prayer books, the Gospel, local maps, a travel pass and a bottle of water to cope with the fierce heat.
They also received police security guidelines.

Dubost said all those attending mass events would be required to carry a security badge, as France is under a two-year-old security plan put in place after a wave of bombings by suspected Algerian Moslem fundamentalists.
Some 7,000 police have been mobilised to supervise crowds at major events like a welcoming ceremony for the Pope at the Eiffel Tower and his Sunday mass in the Bois de Boulogne park.
The festival will open on Tuesday with a mass to be said by Paris archbishop Jean-Marie Lustiger on the Champ de Mars.

Meals were being prepared at a mass kitchen, but due to the young peoples' large numbers, they were expected to get only the scantiest idea of French gastronomy. Monday night's menu was pork roast, raw tomatoes and doughnuts.
